extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of English common law; legal historians; readers of Blackstone's Commentaries
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the legal principles, statutory modifications, and historical practice governing succession to the English crown and the legal status/rights of the queen. Covers parliamentary interventions, vacancies, legitimacy, religion-based qualifications, and distinctions among types of queens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary nature of the crown
rubrics_metrics.description: The crown of England hath been ever an hereditary crown; though subject to limitations by parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone asserts as a general principle that the title to the crown is hereditary, but immediately qualifies that parliamentary limitations and settlements have repeatedly modified or limited that hereditary right (examples throughout chapter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary power to new-model or alter the succession
rubrics_metrics.description: The king and parliament have a right to new-settle, regulate, or alter the succession to the crown (illustrated by multiple statutes and parliamentary settlements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by examples and statutes: 7 Hen. IV. c. 2 (settling inheritance on Henry IV's issue), 1 Edw. IV. c. 1 (post-usurpation indemnities), 25 Hen. VIII. c. 12, 28 Hen. VIII. c. 7, 35 Hen. VIII. c. 1, 1 Mar. p. 2. c. 1, 13 Eliz. c. 1, the Revolution/Convention settlements (William & Mary), and 12 & 13 W. III. c. 2 (Act of Settlement). Blackstone notes parliament often avoided endorsing original titles while exercising power to settle succession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of descent: representation versus proximity of blood
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically uncertain whether the child of an elder brother succeeds by right of representation or whether the younger surviving brother succeeds by right of proximity of blood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone cites historical confusion (e.g., contest in time of Henry II / John) and notes the question remained undecided in some collateral successions (e.g., certain fiefs of the empire). This ambiguity affected claims (e.g., Arthur v. John).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference of entire male line versus female descent
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims have been asserted on the basis that the entire male line should have preference over female lines, or conversely that the crown may descend through females when no male heirs exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone recounts Henry IV's asserted title (preference for the entire male line) contrasted with descent through Philippa (female line) to the house of York. Statutes (e.g., 25 Hen. VIII) and parliamentary settlements have at times entailed succession to male heirs or otherwise regulated female succession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy and bastardy affect succession
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of legitimacy (bastardy or legitimation) materially affect the right to succeed; parliamentary acts could legitimize or bastardize persons, but such acts sometimes expressly reserved the royal dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Richard III's insinuation of Edward IV's children's bastardy to justify usurpation; John of Gaunt's illegitimate offspring were legitimated by act (20 Ric. II) 'to be inheritable to lands' but with an express reservation 'excepta dignitate regali' (except the royal dignity). Statutes in Henry VIII's reign likewise bastardized or legitimated heirs as part of succession settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between de jure and de facto sovereigns and indemnity for acts of usurpers
rubrics_metrics.description: Where succession has been breached by usurpation, Parliament and statute may distinguish 'de facto' rulers from 'de jure' sovereigns and yet confirm and indemnify acts and honours granted by those in possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the York/Lancaster conflicts and usurpations, statute 1 Edw. IV. c. 1 described the three Henrys as 'nuper de facto, et non de jure, reges Angliae.' Parliament confirmed acts of those in possession to secure peace and protect subjects who submitted to the established power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vacancy by abdication and the convention's authority to fill it
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reigning monarch abdicates or the throne becomes vacant, the lords and commons (as trustees/representatives of the nation) have the authority to determine and fill the vacancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone recounts the Revolution of 1688 where a parliamentary convention resolved that James II had 'abdicated the government' and the throne was vacant; the convention then declared William and Mary to be king and queen and prescribed the subsequent order of succession. He reasons there is no other tribunal competent to decide in such a case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary exclusion of particular heirs (e.g., Exclusion Bill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament may enact measures to exclude specific individuals from the succession (illustrated by the Exclusion Bill to set aside the duke of York for being a papist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone uses the Exclusion Bill episode to show two points: (1) the crown was universally acknowledged to be hereditary, and (2) parliament had the power to defeat an inheritance (the commons passed the bill but the lords rejected it and the king would not consent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious qualifications and disqualifications for succession
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory provisions may condition the succession on religious status (e.g., exclusion of Catholics; requirement to join the Church of England; restrictions on marrying Catholics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include statutes around the Revolution (1 W. & M. st. 2. c. 2) making reconciliation with Rome, communion with Rome, or marriage to a papist grounds for exclusion; and 12 & 13 W. III. c. 2 (Act of Settlement) which settled the crown on the electress Sophia and her Protestant heirs, and enacted requirements that future possessors join the communion of the Church of England.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penal sanctions for denying parliamentary authority over succession
rubrics_metrics.description: It was made penal to assert that common law alone (unaltered by parliament) ought to direct the right of the crown, or to deny that the crown can be bound by statutes made with the authority of parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone cites 13 Eliz. c. 1 which made it high treason during the queen's life (and a misdemeanour thereafter) to maintain that parliament could not direct the right of the crown; and 6 Ann. c. 7 which penalized those who maintained that kings with authority of parliament could not make laws binding the descent of the crown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative methods of acquiring the crown (donation/purchase/settlement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The crown may be acquired not only by descent but by donation or 'purchase' (parliamentary/constitutional settlement), whereby persons in possession take by grant rather than strict hereditary right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone explains that William, Mary, and Anne 'did not take the crown by hereditary right or descent, but by way of donation or purchase' effected by the convention and parliament; such settlements could depart from the usual course of descent while retaining some regard for hereditary lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of queens and their legal capacities
rubrics_metrics.description: The queen may be a queen regnant (sovereign), queen consort (wife of reigning king), or queen dowager; a queen regnant has the same powers as a king, while a queen consort possesses distinct legal privileges and a separate legal personality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone: queen regnant (or regent/regnant/sovereign) holds the crown in her own right and has the same powers, prerogatives and duties as a king (statute 1 Mar. I. st. 3. c. 1 cited). The queen consort is a public person distinct from the king: she can purchase and convey lands, take grants from the king, has separate courts and officers, her attorney/solicitor-general may sit within the bar, she may sue and be sued alone, hold separate property in goods and lands, and dispose of them by will (authorities cited: Finch, Justinian).
